after: ## A way to organise this content
alt: Three questions to ask of every actor in globalisation: what resources it has (money, law, votes, people, knowledge), whose interests it serves and who holds it to account.
caption: Ask about resources, interests and accountability, not just names.

alt: More developed states write global rules and, Chang argues, kicked away the ladder; less developed states either compete for investment or act as developmental states like South Korea and Taiwan. A note weighs Ohmae and Strange against continuing state power.
caption: States still shape globalisation, though unequally.

alt: Benefits of TNCs (investment, jobs, technology, markets, tax) set against costs (profits flowing out, footloose production, blurred responsibility), with Bhopal, Rana Plaza and Sklair’s transnational capitalist class.
caption: TNC power is real but can be contested, as the Rana Plaza accord shows.

alt: A grid contrasting the IMF, World Bank and WTO, which use loan conditions and trade rules, with UN agencies such as UNDP, WHO, UNICEF, UNHCR and the ILO, which set norms and deliver services but cannot enforce most targets.
caption: Lenders have leverage; UN agencies mostly set norms.

alt: NGOs with their strengths and weaknesses, grassroots movements such as the Zapatistas, La Via Campesina and Narmada Bachao Andolan, and indigenous peoples with free, prior and informed consent and Standing Rock.
caption: Movements from below use the same global tools as those above.

alt: Four distinctions between types of aid, including tied aid, and the 0.7% target, then arguments for aid (modernisation, Sachs, humanitarian and health aid) and against from the right (Moyo, Easterly) and the left (Hayter).
caption: Distinguish the type of aid before judging whether it helps.
